title: ACCA MA - Management Accounting
content_provenance: Original practice items authored from the ACCA MA syllabus study guide. Not a capture of past exam questions.

items.domain: The Nature, Source and Purpose of Management Information
items.stem: A company prepares statutory financial statements for its shareholders and also monthly cost reports used by its production managers. Which statement best describes the primary purpose of the management accounting reports?
options: To help internal managers plan, control and make decisions
To satisfy the legal reporting requirements of external shareholders
To provide a historical record for tax authorities only
To publish audited results to the stock exchange
items.explanation: Management accounting provides information for internal users so they can plan, control and decide. It is not governed by external reporting standards and is often forward-looking, whereas statutory financial statements and tax filings serve the external reporting purpose.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - The Nature, Source and Purpose of Management Information

items.domain: The Nature, Source and Purpose of Management Information
items.stem: An accountant collects raw figures showing the number of units produced by each machine every day. These figures are then combined into a weekly report that shows average output per machine. Which term best describes the weekly report?
items.explanation: Raw, unprocessed facts are data. Once data has been processed, organised and given meaning for a user it becomes information, so the weekly report of average output is information rather than data.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - The Nature, Source and Purpose of Management Information

items.domain: The Nature, Source and Purpose of Management Information
items.stem: A manager receives a detailed cost report three weeks after the period it covers, by which time the decisions it was meant to support have already been taken. Which quality of good information is most clearly lacking?
items.explanation: Information must be available in time to influence the decision it supports. A report that arrives after the decision has been taken has lost its value even if it is accurate, relevant and complete.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - The Nature, Source and Purpose of Management Information

items.domain: The Nature, Source and Purpose of Management Information
items.stem: A market research team gathers new customer opinions by conducting its own telephone survey rather than using an existing published report. Which source of data does this represent?
items.explanation: Data collected first-hand for the specific purpose in hand is primary data. Secondary data is data that already exists and was collected by someone else, such as a published report or national statistics.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - The Nature, Source and Purpose of Management Information

items.domain: The Nature, Source and Purpose of Management Information
items.stem: A management accountant wants to show how monthly sales revenue has changed over a period of two years and to highlight whether the underlying trend is rising or falling. Which presentation method is most appropriate?
items.explanation: A line graph plots a variable against time and makes trends easy to see. Pie charts show proportions of a total, bar charts compare categories, and scatter diagrams show the relationship between two variables, so none of those highlight a time trend as clearly.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - The Nature, Source and Purpose of Management Information

items.domain: The Nature, Source and Purpose of Management Information
items.stem: A business wants a single integrated software system in which finance, purchasing and inventory all share one database so that each transaction is captured only once. Which type of system is this?
items.explanation: An enterprise resource planning system integrates the main business functions on one shared database, so a transaction entered once updates every affected area. The other options are single-purpose tools that cannot integrate the whole business.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - The Nature, Source and Purpose of Management Information

items.domain: The Nature, Source and Purpose of Management Information
items.stem: An accountant must test a large population of purchase invoices but has limited time. Selecting every twenty-fifth invoice from a numbered list is an example of which sampling method?
items.explanation: Systematic sampling selects items at fixed intervals from an ordered population. Simple random sampling gives every item an equal chance with no fixed interval, stratified sampling first divides the population into groups, and quota sampling is non-random.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - The Nature, Source and Purpose of Management Information

items.domain: The Nature, Source and Purpose of Management Information
items.stem: A manager compares actual monthly expenditure with the budget and investigates any large differences before deciding on corrective action. Which management function does this activity primarily support?
items.explanation: Control is the process of comparing actual performance with plans or budgets and taking corrective action where significant differences arise. Planning looks ahead, and decision making chooses between alternatives, so control best describes the comparison activity.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - The Nature, Source and Purpose of Management Information

items.domain: The Nature, Source and Purpose of Management Information
items.stem: Unlike financial accounting reports prepared for shareholders, management accounting reports are usually characterised in which way?
options: Prepared for internal use and not governed by external reporting standards
Required by law for every limited company
Always audited by an external firm
items.explanation: Management accounting is prepared for internal managers and is not bound by the legal formats or external standards that govern financial reporting. Financial accounting, by contrast, is subject to company law and external audit.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - The Nature, Source and Purpose of Management Information

items.domain: The Nature, Source and Purpose of Management Information
items.stem: A manager wishes to show the proportion of total production cost made up by materials, labour and overheads for a single period. Which presentation method is most suitable?
items.explanation: A pie chart shows how a total is divided into its component parts, so it is ideal for displaying the proportions of a cost total. Line graphs show trends, scatter diagrams show relationships, and Gantt charts show schedules.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - The Nature, Source and Purpose of Management Information

items.stem: A retailer uses the economic order quantity model. Annual demand is 12,000 units, the cost of placing one order is $30 and the annual holding cost per unit is $2. Which amount is closest to the economic order quantity?
items.explanation: Economic order quantity equals the square root of two times annual demand times order cost divided by holding cost, that is the square root of 2 times 12,000 times 30 divided by 2. This gives the square root of 360,000, which is 600 units.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Cost Accounting Techniques

items.stem: A component has a maximum usage of 500 units per week, a minimum usage of 200 units per week, a maximum lead time of 4 weeks and a minimum lead time of 2 weeks. What is the reorder level?
items.explanation: The reorder level anticipates the worst case by using maximum usage and maximum lead time. Multiplying 500 units per week by 4 weeks gives 2,000 units, the level at which a new order should be placed.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Cost Accounting Techniques

items.stem: A store uses the FIFO method of material valuation. Opening inventory is 100 units at $5 each. On 5 May, 200 units are purchased at $6 each, and on 10 May, 150 units are issued. What is the value of the issue on 10 May?
items.explanation: FIFO issues the oldest materials first, so the 150 units come from the opening 100 units at $5 and 50 of the newer units at $6. That is 500 plus 300, a total of $800.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Cost Accounting Techniques

items.stem: A store uses the weighted average cost method. Opening inventory is 200 units valued at $1,000. A purchase of 300 units is then made for $1,800. What is the weighted average cost per unit after the purchase, to the nearest cent?
items.explanation: The weighted average cost is the total cost divided by the total units. Total cost is 1,000 plus 1,800, which is 2,800, and total units are 200 plus 300, which is 500, so the average is $5.60 per unit.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Cost Accounting Techniques

items.stem: An employee is paid a straight piece rate of $2.50 for every unit produced and completes 320 units in a week. What is the employee's gross pay for the week?
items.explanation: Under a straight piece rate the pay depends only on output. Multiplying 320 units by $2.50 per unit gives gross pay of $800.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Cost Accounting Techniques

items.stem: A factory worker is paid a basic rate of $12 per hour for a standard 40-hour week, with an overtime premium of 50 percent for any hours beyond 40. The worker records 46 hours in the week. What is the total wage cost for the week?
items.explanation: Basic pay is 40 hours at $12, which is $480. The overtime rate is $18 per hour, so 6 overtime hours cost $108. Adding them gives a total wage cost of $588.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Cost Accounting Techniques

items.stem: At an activity level of 4,000 units a cost centre's total cost is $30,000, and at 6,000 units its total cost is $40,000. Using the high-low method, what is the variable cost per unit?
items.explanation: The high-low method divides the change in total cost by the change in activity. The change in cost is 40,000 minus 30,000, which is 10,000, and the change in activity is 2,000 units, so the variable cost is $5.00 per unit.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Cost Accounting Techniques

items.stem: Budgeted production overhead is $120,000 and budgeted machine hours are 30,000. Actual overhead incurred is $128,000 and actual machine hours are 31,000. Using a machine-hour absorption rate, what is the amount of overhead over- or under-absorbed?
items.explanation: The absorption rate is 120,000 divided by 30,000, which is $4 per machine hour. Absorbed overhead is 31,000 hours at $4, which is $124,000, and actual overhead is $128,000, so overhead is under-absorbed by $4,000.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Cost Accounting Techniques

items.stem: A company is introducing activity-based costing. Which cost driver would be most appropriate to attach to the activity of setting up production machines?
items.explanation: Activity-based costing links each activity's cost to the factor that drives it. Set-up costs are driven by the number of set-ups or production runs, not by machine hours, labour hours or units produced, which drive other activities.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Cost Accounting Techniques

items.stem: A product sells for $50, its variable cost is $30 per unit and fixed costs total $60,000 per month. What is the contribution per unit?
items.explanation: Contribution per unit is the selling price less the variable cost per unit. Subtracting $30 from $50 gives $20, which is the amount each unit contributes towards fixed costs and profit.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Cost Accounting Techniques

items.stem: A product has a selling price of $50, a variable cost of $30 per unit and total fixed costs of $60,000. What is the break-even point in units?
items.explanation: Contribution per unit is $20, and break-even units equal fixed costs divided by contribution per unit. Dividing $60,000 by $20 gives 3,000 units.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Cost Accounting Techniques

items.stem: A company's break-even sales are $200,000 and its current sales are $250,000. What is the margin of safety expressed as a percentage of current sales?
items.explanation: Margin of safety is current sales less break-even sales, which is $50,000, divided by current sales of $250,000. This gives 20 percent, the amount by which sales can fall before a loss arises.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Cost Accounting Techniques

items.stem: A product makes a contribution of $8 per unit. Fixed costs are $40,000 and the company wants to earn a profit of $16,000. How many units must be sold to achieve this target profit?
items.explanation: To find the target sales volume, add fixed costs and target profit then divide by contribution per unit. Fixed costs of $40,000 plus profit of $16,000 is $56,000, which divided by $8 gives 7,000 units.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Cost Accounting Techniques

items.stem: Two products use the same scarce machine. Product X earns a contribution of $12 per unit and needs 3 machine hours per unit. Product Y earns $16 per unit and needs 5 machine hours per unit. Which product should the company prioritise to maximise total contribution?
options: Product Y, because its contribution per unit is higher
Product Y, because it earns $3.20 of contribution per machine hour
Neither product, as the machine is a fixed cost
Product X, because it earns $4.00 of contribution per machine hour
items.explanation: When a resource is scarce, products should be ranked by contribution per unit of the scarce resource. Product X gives $12 divided by 3, which is $4.00 per machine hour, while Product Y gives $16 divided by 5, which is $3.20, so Product X is preferred.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Cost Accounting Techniques

items.stem: A company has already spent $15,000 on market research for a proposed new product and is now deciding whether to launch it. In a relevant costing decision, how should the $15,000 already spent be treated?
options: It should be ignored because it is a sunk cost
It should be included as a future cash outflow
It should be treated as an opportunity cost
It should be deducted from the product's contribution
items.explanation: Relevant costs are future, incremental cash flows. The $15,000 has already been spent and cannot be changed by the decision, so it is a sunk cost and is ignored. An opportunity cost is a benefit forgone by choosing one option over another.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Cost Accounting Techniques

items.stem: A process has 1,000 units of closing work in progress that are 60 percent complete as to conversion costs. Under the weighted average method, how many equivalent units of conversion cost are represented by this closing work in progress?
items.explanation: Equivalent units measure the work done as if it were fully complete. Multiplying 1,000 units by the 60 percent degree of completion gives 600 equivalent units of conversion cost.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Cost Accounting Techniques

items.stem: In a period when inventory levels are rising, which of the following describes the effect on reported profit of using absorption costing rather than marginal costing?
options: Both methods report identical profits regardless of inventory changes
Absorption costing reports a higher profit because variable costs are excluded
Absorption costing reports a higher profit because some fixed production overhead is carried forward in closing inventory
Absorption costing reports a lower profit because fixed overhead is expensed immediately
items.explanation: Under absorption costing part of the fixed production overhead is held in closing inventory rather than charged to cost of sales. When inventory rises, more fixed overhead is carried forward, so absorption profit exceeds marginal costing profit.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Cost Accounting Techniques

items.stem: A factory's rent and rates cost of $90,000 is to be apportioned between two departments that occupy floor areas of 4,000 square metres and 2,000 square metres. How much of the cost should be apportioned to the larger department if floor area is the basis?
items.explanation: Apportionment spreads a shared cost on a fair basis. Total floor area is 6,000 square metres, so the larger department takes 4,000 divided by 6,000, which is two thirds of $90,000, giving $60,000.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Cost Accounting Techniques

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the purpose of preparing a cash budget?
options: To forecast the timing of cash receipts and payments so that future surpluses or deficits can be anticipated
To calculate the profit earned on each unit sold
To record the historic cost of non-current assets
To replace the need for a statement of financial position
items.explanation: A cash budget forecasts the timing of cash inflows and outflows so that management can plan for surpluses or arrange finance for deficits. It deals with liquidity and timing, not with profit measurement or asset recording.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Budgeting

items.stem: Which budgeting approach starts from a zero base and requires every cost to be justified afresh in each budgeting period?
items.explanation: Zero-based budgeting begins each period with no committed costs and requires every activity and cost to be justified from scratch. Incremental budgeting adjusts last period's figures, while rolling and flexible budgeting address other planning needs.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Budgeting

items.stem: A company updates its budget every quarter by adding a new quarter and dropping the earliest one, so that the budget always covers the next twelve months. Which approach is this?
items.explanation: A rolling or continuous budget is continually updated by adding a new period as the earliest one expires, keeping the planning horizon constant. Zero-based and incremental budgeting concern how costs are determined, not how the horizon is maintained.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Budgeting

items.stem: A company plans to sell 10,000 units next month. It expects to hold 800 units in opening finished goods inventory and wants 1,500 units in closing inventory. How many units must it produce?
items.explanation: Production equals budgeted sales plus required closing inventory less opening inventory. That is 10,000 plus 1,500 less 800, giving 10,700 units to be produced.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Budgeting

items.stem: A company will produce 10,700 units next month and each unit uses 2 kilograms of material. Opening material inventory is 1,000 kilograms and the required closing inventory is 1,400 kilograms. How many kilograms of material must be purchased?
items.explanation: Material usage is 10,700 units times 2 kilograms, which is 21,400 kilograms. Purchases equal usage plus closing inventory less opening inventory, that is 21,400 plus 1,400 less 1,000, giving 21,800 kilograms.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Budgeting

items.stem: Credit sales for January were $50,000. Customers are expected to pay 60 percent in the following month and the remaining 40 percent in the month after that. What amount of cash from January sales is received in March?
items.explanation: January sales are collected 60 percent in February and 40 percent in March. The March receipt from January sales is therefore 40 percent of $50,000, which is $20,000.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Budgeting

items.stem: A company budgets variable production cost at $6 per unit and fixed production cost at $20,000 per month. What total production cost should appear in a flexible budget prepared for 5,000 units?
items.explanation: A flexible budget allows variable cost to change with the activity level while fixed cost stays constant. Variable cost is 5,000 units at $6, which is $30,000, and adding fixed cost of $20,000 gives $50,000.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Budgeting

items.stem: Which of the following is the main behavioural advantage claimed for participative (bottom-up) budgeting?
options: It is always quicker to prepare than top-down budgeting
It guarantees the elimination of all budget slack
It removes the need for a master budget
It can increase managers' commitment and motivation because they helped set the targets
items.explanation: When managers take part in setting their own budgets they tend to be more committed to achieving them. Participation is not necessarily quicker and it can even encourage budget slack, so it does not remove the need for a master budget.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Budgeting

items.stem: Which budget is normally prepared first when building a master budget for a manufacturing business, because the activity levels in most other budgets depend on it?
items.explanation: The sales budget is the starting point because production, materials, labour and other functional budgets all depend on the expected level of sales. The cash budget is usually prepared later, once the other budgets are known.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Budgeting

items.stem: A manager deliberately overstates the costs in a budget bid so that the resulting budget target will be easier to achieve. What is this behaviour normally called?
items.explanation: Budget slack, or budgetary padding, is the deliberate understatement of revenue or overstatement of costs to make a budget easier to meet. A favourable variance is an actual-versus-budget outcome, not the padding itself.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Budgeting

items.stem: The first unit of a new product takes 100 hours to make. An 80 percent learning curve applies, so the cumulative average time per unit falls to 80 percent of its previous level each time output doubles. What is the time taken to make the second unit?
items.explanation: With an 80 percent learning curve the cumulative average for two units is 80 percent of 100, which is 80 hours. Total time for two units is 160 hours, so the second unit takes 160 less the first 100, which is 60 hours.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Budgeting

items.stem: A time series is decomposed additively into trend, seasonal variation and residual variation. If the trend and seasonal components have been identified, what does the residual variation represent?
options: A repeatable pattern within each year
The long-term underlying direction of the data
The difference between budget and actual results
Random or irregular movements not explained by trend or season
items.explanation: Once the trend and seasonal components are removed from the data, what remains is the residual, which represents random or irregular influences. The seasonal pattern is a separate component, and the trend is the long-term direction.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Budgeting

items.stem: A company purchased 5,000 kilograms of material at $9.50 per kilogram when the standard price is $10.00 per kilogram. What is the material price variance?
items.explanation: The material price variance is the difference between standard and actual price multiplied by the quantity purchased. The standard price is $0.50 higher than the actual price, so 5,000 kilograms at $0.50 gives a favourable variance of $2,500.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Standard Costing and Performance Measurement

items.stem: A product should use 3 kilograms of material per unit at a standard price of $10 per kilogram. The company produced 1,000 units and used 3,200 kilograms in total. What is the material usage variance?
items.explanation: Standard material for the actual output is 1,000 units times 3 kilograms, which is 3,000 kilograms. The company used 200 kilograms more than standard, and 200 at the standard price of $10 gives an adverse usage variance of $2,000.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Standard Costing and Performance Measurement

items.stem: A company paid its workforce for 2,000 hours at an actual rate of $11 per hour for work whose standard rate is $10 per hour. What is the labour rate variance?
items.explanation: The labour rate variance is the difference between standard and actual rate multiplied by the hours paid. The actual rate is $1 higher than standard, so 2,000 hours at $1 gives an adverse variance of $2,000.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Standard Costing and Performance Measurement

items.stem: A product has a standard labour time of 0.5 hours per unit at a standard rate of $12 per hour. The company produced 3,000 units using 1,600 labour hours. What is the labour efficiency variance?
items.explanation: Standard hours for the actual output are 3,000 units times 0.5 hours, which is 1,500 hours. The company used 100 hours more than standard, and 100 hours at the standard rate of $12 gives an adverse efficiency variance of $1,200.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Standard Costing and Performance Measurement

items.stem: Budgeted variable overhead is $5 per labour hour. Actual labour hours worked were 1,600 and actual variable overhead expenditure was $8,400. What is the variable overhead expenditure variance?
items.explanation: The expected variable overhead for the actual hours is 1,600 hours at $5, which is $8,000. Actual expenditure was $8,400, so the company spent $400 more than expected, giving an adverse variance of $400.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Standard Costing and Performance Measurement

items.stem: Budgeted fixed overheads for a period are $50,000 and the actual fixed overheads incurred are $47,000. What is the fixed overhead expenditure variance?
items.explanation: The fixed overhead expenditure variance compares actual fixed overhead with the budget. Actual cost of $47,000 is $3,000 below the budget of $50,000, so the variance is $3,000 favourable.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Standard Costing and Performance Measurement

items.stem: A company expected to sell 4,000 units at a standard selling price of $25 each. It actually sold 4,200 units at $24 each. What is the sales price variance?
items.explanation: The sales price variance is the difference between actual and standard price multiplied by actual units sold. The actual price is $1 below standard, and 4,200 units at $1 gives an adverse variance of $4,200.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Standard Costing and Performance Measurement

items.stem: The standard contribution per unit of a product is $8. Budgeted sales volume is 5,000 units and actual sales volume is 5,400 units. What is the sales volume contribution variance?
items.explanation: The sales volume contribution variance is the difference between actual and budgeted sales volume multiplied by standard contribution per unit. The company sold 400 units more than budget, and 400 at $8 gives a favourable variance of $3,200.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Standard Costing and Performance Measurement

items.stem: A division reports an operating profit of $60,000 and net assets of $400,000. What is the division's return on investment?
items.explanation: Return on investment is operating profit divided by the net assets employed. Dividing $60,000 by $400,000 gives 0.15, which is 15 percent.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Standard Costing and Performance Measurement

items.stem: A division earns an operating profit of $60,000 on net assets of $400,000. The company applies an imputed interest charge of 10 percent on net assets. What is the division's residual income?
items.explanation: Residual income is operating profit less the imputed interest charge on net assets. The charge is 10 percent of $400,000, which is $40,000, and subtracting that from $60,000 leaves residual income of $20,000.
items.reference: ACCA MA Syllabus Study Guide - Standard Costing and Performance Measurement
